regions.name: Virginia
regions.summary: Virginia reaches from the Chesapeake Bay on the mid-Atlantic coast west over the Blue Ridge into the Appalachians, and its wine story runs from the Jamestown law of 1619 that told every householder to plant ten vines, through Thomas Jefferson's failed vineyards at Monticello, to a modern industry built since the 1970s. Its problem is not winter cold, as in New York, but heat, humidity and summer rain, which bring rot and mildew. Viognier, promoted as its signature grape since 2011, and Cabernet Franc lead, with Petit Manseng, Petit Verdot, Chardonnay, Bordeaux blends and the native Norton beside them. Monticello, around Charlottesville, is the AVA a server meets first.

terroir.climate: Humid subtropical in the Tidewater and the Piedmont, cooler and more continental in the Blue Ridge and the Shenandoah Valley. Summers are hot and humid, with frequent thunderstorms, and rain can fall in any month, harvest included, when the remnants of Atlantic hurricanes may arrive in September and October. Winters in the mountains and the Valley can be cold enough to injure vines, and spring frost follows an early bud break. Humidity, not cold, is the grower's enemy: downy and powdery mildew, black rot and bunch rot press all season, and Pierce's disease, carried by insects, threatens vinifera in the warm south-east.
terroir.soils: The Piedmont and the Blue Ridge foothills, where most vineyards lie, have deep, weathered clay and clay loam, often red with iron, over granite, gneiss, schist and the old volcanic greenstone of the Blue Ridge; the clay holds water and pushes vigour, so growers prize the rockier, better drained hillsides. The Shenandoah Valley rests on limestone and shale, and the Coastal Plain in the east on sand, silt and loam laid down by the sea and the rivers.
terroir.topography: The state rises from the flat Coastal Plain along the Chesapeake Bay, the Tidewater, over the rolling Piedmont to the Blue Ridge Mountains, and beyond them to the Shenandoah Valley and the Alleghenies on the border with West Virginia. Most vineyards sit in the Piedmont and on the eastern foothills of the Blue Ridge, on slopes and hilltops chosen so that cold air and damp air drain away from the vines.
terroir.water: The Chesapeake Bay and the Atlantic warm the Eastern Shore and the Tidewater, lengthen their season and soften their winters, but add to the humidity. The broad tidal rivers, the Potomac, the Rappahannock, the York and the James, cross the Coastal Plain to the bay and frame the Northern Neck and the Virginia Peninsula. In the west the Shenandoah River drains north through its valley to join the Potomac at Harpers Ferry.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Promoted by the Virginia Wine Board as the state's signature grape from 2011: full, round, dry whites of apricot, peach and honeysuckle, sometimes with a touch of oak.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: The red that copes with the humid season and ripens before Cabernet Sauvignon: medium bodied, fragrant reds of red fruit, herbs and graphite, alone or in blends.

grapes.name: Petit Manseng
grapes.styles: Jurançon's grape, whose thick skins and loose bunches resist rot: it holds high acidity at high sugar, for dry, off dry and sweet whites of pineapple and citrus.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: Ripens fully in the long, warm season: deep, violet-scented reds bottled alone, and the colour and spine of many blends.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Planted widely: oaked and unoaked whites, and a base for traditional method sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Softens the Bordeaux-style blends, with Cabernet Sauvignon on warm, well drained sites.

grapes.name: Norton
grapes.styles: A native American vine raised in Richmond in the 1820s and resistant to the diseases of the humid east: dark, high-acid, low-tannin reds with a wild, grapey note.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.styles: Thick skinned and suited to humidity: crisp, saline whites from a small but spreading planting.

grapes.name: Vidal Blanc
grapes.styles: A hardy French-American hybrid for fresh whites and late harvest wines; Chambourcin is its red counterpart.

wines.note: Full bodied and dry, with apricot, peach, honeysuckle and a little bitterness on the finish; serve it with crab cakes, roast chicken or mildly spiced dishes.
Medium bodied, with red cherry, raspberry, dried herbs and graphite and moderate tannin; serve it slightly cool with pork, duck or a ham supper.
Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Petit Verdot and Cabernet Sauvignon together: dark fruit, cedar and firm tannin from French oak; decant it and pour it with steak or lamb.
Dry to sweet, with pineapple, citrus and honey and a streak of high acidity; the off dry style suits spicy food, the sweet one fruit desserts.
Inky and juicy, with dark berries, spice and a wild note, high in acid and soft in tannin; a match for barbecue and smoked meats.
Traditional method wine from Chardonnay, sometimes with Pinot Noir: crisp, citrus and brioche; an aperitif or a glass with oysters.

made.viticulture: Everything turns on the humid summer. Growers choose slopes and hilltops where air moves and cold air drains away, train most vines with vertically positioned shoots, pull leaves around the bunches for air and sun, and spray through the season against downy and powdery mildew and black rot. The deep clay pushes vigour, so cover crops between the rows, low vigour rootstocks and careful canopy work keep the vines in balance. Grapes are chosen for thick skins and loose bunches that resist rot: Petit Manseng, Petit Verdot, Cabernet Franc and the native Norton. Vinifera is grafted against phylloxera, which is native to eastern North America and, with the fungal diseases, killed the European vines of the colonial era and of Jefferson's Monticello. Late spring frost after an early bud break, winter injury in the Valley and the mountains, and the tail of a hurricane at harvest are the other hazards, so picking is often timed by the forecast as much as by ripeness.
made.winemaking: Most Virginia wine is made by small estates in a broadly French idiom. Viognier is fermented in steel or older barrels, sometimes stirred on its lees for texture, and kept dry. Cabernet Franc and the Bordeaux varieties are destemmed, fermented warm with pumping over or punching down, and aged in French oak; the leading reds are blends, in which Petit Verdot and Merlot add colour and flesh. Petit Manseng's high acidity lets it be made dry, off dry or as a late harvest sweet wine. Norton is made as a dry red, its acidity softened by malolactic conversion and time in oak. A few estates make traditional method sparkling wine. In a wet vintage, sorting out damaged fruit and gentle extraction matter more than chasing ripeness, and the hybrids Vidal Blanc and Chambourcin give dependable wine when vinifera struggles.

law.classification: Virginia's wine law is the federal one. An AVA states origin only: a wine naming one takes at least 85 per cent of its grapes from it, a varietal wine at least 75 per cent of the named grape, and a vintage on an AVA wine at least 95 per cent from that year. A wine labelled Virginia takes at least 75 per cent of its grapes from the state under federal law. The AVAs lying wholly or partly in the state include Monticello around Charlottesville; the Shenandoah Valley, shared with West Virginia; Middleburg Virginia, approved in 2012; Virginia Peninsula, approved in 2021; the Northern Neck George Washington Birthplace; Virginia's Eastern Shore; Rocky Knob and the North Fork of Roanoke in the south-west; and the Appalachian High Country, shared with North Carolina and Tennessee. The Virginia Wine Board, a state body, funds research and promotion and chose Viognier as the signature grape in 2011, a marketing choice rather than a law.
tiers: At least 75 per cent of the grapes from Virginia under federal law.
Origin only: at least 85 per cent of the grapes from the named area; no rule on grape, yield or ageing.
The Piedmont and Blue Ridge foothills around Charlottesville, named for Jefferson's estate.
The valley between the Blue Ridge and the Alleghenies, shared with West Virginia; it holds the bare name, so California's is California Shenandoah Valley.
2012: parts of Loudoun and Fauquier counties in Northern Virginia, west of Washington.
2021: the land between the James and the York around Williamsburg.
labels: A registered name for a blend of Bordeaux grapes, licensed to member wineries; common on Virginia's red blends.
Federal: grapes from the winery's own or controlled vineyards in the named AVA, made and bottled there.
A native American grape raised in Richmond; the same variety is sold as Cynthiana in some states.
Jurançon's grape, grown in Virginia for dry, off dry and sweet whites; read the label for the style.
A state licence for a winery that grows fruit and sells directly to the public, not an appellation.

places.name: Monticello
places.note: The AVA of the Piedmont and the eastern Blue Ridge foothills around Charlottesville, named for Jefferson's hilltop house: the historic heart of Virginia wine, where Filippo Mazzei planted for Jefferson in the 1770s and where Viognier, Cabernet Franc and Petit Manseng do well today.

places.name: Northern Virginia
places.note: Loudoun and Fauquier counties west of Washington, in the foothills of the Blue Ridge and the Bull Run Mountains: a large cluster of estates within reach of the capital, known for Bordeaux blends, Cabernet Franc and Petit Manseng.

places.name: Middleburg Virginia
places.note: The AVA of 2012 around the horse country town of Middleburg in Loudoun and Fauquier counties, petitioned by Boxwood Winery: rolling hills of weathered rock, Bordeaux grapes and Cabernet Franc.

places.name: Shenandoah Valley
places.note: The limestone valley between the Blue Ridge and the Alleghenies, an AVA shared with West Virginia, sheltered and drier than the Piedmont with colder winters. In the early 1980s it kept the bare name, so California's AVA in Amador County became California Shenandoah Valley.

places.name: The Coastal Plain
places.note: The low, sandy Tidewater along the Chesapeake Bay and the Atlantic: long, warm, humid seasons, mild winters and the bay's breezes.

places.name: Virginia Peninsula
places.note: The AVA of 2021 between the James and the York rivers around Williamsburg, petitioned by the Williamsburg Winery; sandy soils and a long, warm season.

places.name: Northern Neck George Washington Birthplace
places.note: One AVA, not two: the peninsula between the Potomac and the Rappahannock, named for Washington's birthplace in Westmoreland County.

places.name: Virginia's Eastern Shore
places.note: The Virginia tip of the Delmarva Peninsula between the Chesapeake Bay and the Atlantic, a flat, sandy, sea-tempered AVA.

places.name: The south-west
places.note: The Blue Ridge plateau and the Appalachian valleys of south-western Virginia, higher, cooler and more continental than the Piedmont, with small, scattered vineyards.

places.name: Rocky Knob
places.note: A small AVA on the Blue Ridge plateau in Floyd and Patrick counties, at altitude, with cool nights.

places.name: North Fork of Roanoke
places.note: The valley of the Roanoke River's north fork in Montgomery and Roanoke counties, a small AVA between the ridges.

places.name: Appalachian High Country
places.note: A mountain AVA shared with North Carolina and Tennessee, cold in winter, for hardy hybrids and a few vinifera.

producers.name: Barboursville Vineyards
producers.why: Founded in 1976 by a Veneto wine family beside the ruins of a house Jefferson designed, a pioneer of vinifera in the state; known for its Bordeaux blend Octagon and for Italian grapes.

producers.name: Horton Vineyards
producers.why: An Orange County estate that led Virginia's turn to Viognier and championed Norton and Petit Manseng.

producers.name: Linden Vineyards
producers.why: A Blue Ridge estate in Fauquier County known for site-driven Bordeaux blends and Chardonnay from its mountain slopes.

producers.name: Jefferson Vineyards
producers.why: A Charlottesville estate on the land near Monticello where Mazzei planted for Jefferson in the 1770s.

producers.name: Boxwood Winery
producers.why: A Middleburg estate making Bordeaux-style blends, whose petition created the Middleburg Virginia AVA in 2012.

producers.name: The Williamsburg Winery
producers.why: A Virginia Peninsula estate whose petition created the Virginia Peninsula AVA in 2021.

producers.name: Chrysalis Vineyards
producers.why: A Northern Virginia estate known for its devotion to Norton and for Albariño.

exam: Place Virginia on the mid-Atlantic coast, south of Washington, with most vineyards in the Piedmont and the Blue Ridge foothills.
Know its problem: heat, humidity and summer rain bringing rot and mildew, with hurricane remnants at harvest, not winter cold as in New York.
Name its grapes: Viognier and Cabernet Franc first, then Petit Manseng, Petit Verdot, Chardonnay, the Bordeaux blends and the native Norton.
Hold the history: the Jamestown law of 1619 and its ten vines, Jefferson's failed vineyards at Monticello with Mazzei, Norton raised in Richmond in the 1820s, the revival from the 1970s.
Know Monticello as the AVA around Charlottesville, and the Shenandoah Valley as the AVA that kept the bare name, so California's is California Shenandoah Valley.
Apply the federal label rules: 75 per cent of the named grape, 85 per cent from an AVA, 75 per cent from Virginia for the state name.
Asked from Premier Cru: Middleburg Virginia (2012) and Virginia Peninsula (2021), and the Shenandoah Valley AVA shared with West Virginia.
Asked from Grand Cru: the smaller AVAs, Northern Neck George Washington Birthplace, Virginia's Eastern Shore, Rocky Knob, North Fork of Roanoke and the Appalachian High Country.
traps: Virginia's Shenandoah Valley holds the bare name; California's, in Amador County, is California Shenandoah Valley.
Viognier as the signature grape (2011) was the Virginia Wine Board's marketing choice, not a state law.
Jefferson never made a lasting wine from his vines at Monticello; his European vines failed to disease and phylloxera.
Norton is an American vine of the 1820s, older than the French-American hybrids such as Vidal Blanc and Chambourcin, and the same variety is sold as Cynthiana in some states.
Virginia's vintage is decided by humidity and rain, not by winter cold as in the Finger Lakes.
Northern Neck George Washington Birthplace is the name of one AVA, not two.
A Virginia Petit Manseng may be dry or sweet: the grape holds its acidity at high sugar, so the label, not the grape, says the style.

cards.b: Viognier and Cabernet Franc lead; then Petit Manseng, Petit Verdot, Chardonnay, Merlot in Bordeaux-style blends, the native Norton, and hybrids such as Vidal Blanc and Chambourcin.

Humidity and summer rain: downy and powdery mildew, black rot and bunch rot, with hurricane remnants at harvest and Pierce's disease in the warm south-east. Winter cold matters only in the mountains and the Valley.
The first General Assembly, sitting at Jamestown, ordered every householder to plant and keep ten vines each year.
In the 1770s Jefferson backed Filippo Mazzei's Italian vineyard beside Monticello; the European vines failed to disease and phylloxera, and Jefferson never made a lasting wine.
A native American vine raised in Richmond in the 1820s, sold as Norton's Virginia Seedling; disease resistant, it makes dark, high-acid, low-tannin red.
Chosen as the state's signature grape by the Virginia Wine Board in 2011, a marketing title: full, dry whites of apricot, peach and honeysuckle.
Virginia's kept the bare name in the early 1980s; California's, in Amador County, must be called California Shenandoah Valley.

cards.f: Petit Manseng in Virginia: why it suits
cards.b: Thick skins and loose bunches resist rot in the humid summer, and it keeps high acidity at high sugar, so it is made dry, off dry or sweet.
Middleburg Virginia (2012), in Loudoun and Fauquier counties west of Washington; Virginia Peninsula (2021), between the James and the York around Williamsburg.
Northern Neck George Washington Birthplace, Virginia's Eastern Shore, Rocky Knob, North Fork of Roanoke, and the Appalachian High Country shared with North Carolina and Tennessee.

questions.q: Which white grape did the Virginia Wine Board choose as the state's signature grape in 2011?
questions.exp: Viognier was named the signature grape in 2011, a marketing choice. Chardonnay is planted widely, Petit Manseng is rising, and Albariño is a newer arrival.

questions.q: Which red grape, paired with Viognier, has built Virginia's modern reputation?
questions.exp: Cabernet Franc ripens before Cabernet Sauvignon and copes with the humid season; Cabernet Sauvignon needs warm sites, Pinot Noir struggles with rot, and Zinfandel belongs to California.

questions.q: How many vines did the Jamestown law of 1619 order every householder to plant each year?
questions.exp: The first General Assembly of Virginia, meeting at Jamestown in 1619, ordered every householder to plant and keep ten vines each year.

questions.q: Which native American grape was raised in Richmond in the 1820s?
questions.exp: Norton, sold as Norton's Virginia Seedling, came from Richmond. Concord was raised in Massachusetts, Catawba spread from the Carolinas, and Scuppernong is a muscadine of the south.

questions.q: What is the chief threat to Virginia's vineyards during the growing season?
questions.exp: Hot, humid summers and frequent rain bring downy and powdery mildew, black rot and bunch rot; winter cold matters only in the mountains and the Valley.

questions.q: Which AVA, named for Thomas Jefferson's estate, surrounds Charlottesville?
questions.exp: The Monticello AVA covers the Piedmont and Blue Ridge foothills around Charlottesville, where Jefferson and Mazzei tried European vines in the 1770s.

questions.q: Which state shares the Shenandoah Valley AVA with Virginia?
questions.exp: The valley runs north across the state line into West Virginia, and the AVA covers both. North Carolina shares the Appalachian High Country instead.

questions.q: Which Virginia AVA lies on the peninsula between the Potomac and the Rappahannock rivers?
accept: Northern Neck George Washington Birthplace AVA
questions.exp: The Northern Neck George Washington Birthplace AVA is named for Washington's birthplace in Westmoreland County, on the peninsula between the two rivers.
